Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which affects all hon. members of this house. It concerns a motion which was placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) relating to the production of a certain list of instructions, or what have you, to the members of the cabinet by the Postmaster General (Mr. Denis). The Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) and the Postmaster General have both denied the existence of this list, and in reply to the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North for the production of this list a nil return was tabled.
The matter has also to do with the statement of Your Honour in this house yesterday. Subsequent to the transpiration of these events, namely the denial of the Secretary of State and the Postmaster General of the existence of this document, and subsequent to the statement by Your Honour in the house yesterday, certain events took place last night which I think justify the reopening of the whole matter. Your Honour's statement dealt with the propriety of a private member tabling a document which was in his possession, and also dealt with the denials of the Postmaster General and the Secretary of State.
Last night, while Your Honour was absent from the chair, the matter of this list again arose. Your Honour will find recorded on pages 3882 and 3883 of last night's proceedings the undoubted admission by the Postmaster General that this list actually is in existence. Only one of these statements can be true. Either the document exists or it does not exist. We on this side of the house are convinced it does exist. I feel that since the remarks of the Postmaster General last night give a clear indication that the document does exist, there has been a deliberate misleading of the members of this house both by the Postmaster General and the Secretary of State.
Because of the very fundamental questions involved here, including the integrity of two cabinet ministers and the privileges of every
hon. member in this house, in my view and in the view of several other members on this side of the house the matter deserves a more careful inquiry than it has received. We feel that these denials have been false. There should be an opportunity given to the members of this house to determine whether or not the document exists.
I move, therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler):
That the matters raised in the statement made to the house this day-
That is October 22.
-be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections, and that such committee be instructed to report its findings thereon to the house.

I begin by saying that I am not enthused about sending this matter to the committee in the light of what happened to the last deliberations of that committee and the way the house changed the spirit of the recommendations made by that committee. I should like, however, to say something about this matter because it arises out of a motion for the production of papers which I moved last week. This motion was to the effect that an order of the house be issued for a list of consultants prepared in the office of the Postmaster General for the guidance of cabinet ministers, and copies of all correspondence between ministers of the crown and the consultants in each riding.
Sessional paper 243, dated October 17, 1963, the return of the Postmaster General to this motion No. 99, was to the effect there was no such list and, therefore, no such correspondence. Now, it seems obvious to me that what I was asking for was a list prepared by the Postmaster General, or at least in his department, and used by the minister or other cabinet ministers. I think that was pretty obvious. The minister said in his reply that there was no such list and, therefore, no such correspondence. Last night in this house the minister said a number of things, one of which, as reported on page 3883 of Hansard, was as follows:
This document is a personal document to speed up the work. It is in order to prepare letters for my signature.

Question of Privilege
When the minister says "this document" he is in fact admitting that there is such a document, a fact which he denied in his return. Later on, as reported at page 3884 of Hansard, he said:
I might say that this document is for my personal use-
Yet, Mr. Speaker, in his return he said in fact there was no document and there had been no correspondence with any of the people concerned, the consultants mentioned. In the Winnipeg Tribune of October 8, 1963 there is a story concerning Rev. Fred Douglas, who was the Liberal candidate in the constituency of Winnipeg South Centre, and listing Mr. Douglas as the consultant in the constituency. Mr. Douglas is quoted as saying:
For the best information possible it seems logical that the government in power should continue to consult its constituency organizations-whichever government that happened to be.
Mr. Douglas has been listed as a consultant for his riding. Asked if he was in fact a consultant, Mr. Douglas said:
I am interested in the constituency and its welfare, and from time to time write letters. If people in the constituency want something I may bring it to the attention of the government.
Mr. Douglas said that he received notice that a new postal station was being considered and was asked if he knew anyone in the area suitable for the job. Here is a statement, Mr. Speaker, by a Liberal candidate in the last election to the effect that he was in fact written to by the department in connection with a postal station in the constituency. Yet in his return the minister said that there was no such list and no correspondence.
I do not know what good it will do to send this matter to the committee, Mr. Speaker. It seems to me that if members of parliament cannot get ministers to give an honest and forthright answer to questions asked of them it is going to be virtually impossible for this house to do the business which the members have been sent here to do. Surely the basis for a parliamentary system such as we have is that if a member of parliament asks a minister a question he should get an honest answer. You yourself, Mr. Speaker, and I think rightly so, last week insisted that a minister's statement must be accepted as being factual. Hon. members on this side would like to be able to follow this position and to know that when they ask a question and receive an answer the answer does contain all the facts. If as we go along we find out this is not so we will have no alternative but to continue to cross-examine and badger ministers, and I think this will certainly affect the work of

However, a question of privilege has been raised. I have given some thought to the questions raised last night and to the question of privilege raised today. It is, of course, my duty to say whether there is a prima facie case before I consider the motion moved by the hon. member for Yukon. If I may clear up some points of confusion I think it might be useful at this time to make a reasonably short statement to the house on how the Chair sees the matter.
At the opening of yesterday's sitting, I presented to the house my views concerning a question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce in relation to the existence of a document in the office of the Postmaster General.

I may briefly summarize my views in regard to that question of privilege by saying that in my opinion the matter was, in effect, a dispute between two members as to allegations of facts and, therefore, a prima facie breach of privilege did not arise in regard thereto.
Last evening, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre rose on a question of privilege in relation to the same matter and, as reported at pages 3884-5 of Hansard, stated in part as follows:
I realize that you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, are in the chair at the moment, but my point of privilege is that in all fairness to all the members of this house his honour the Speaker must now reconsider this matter and report again to the house upon it. We have been told by him we have to take the minister's word and that the hon. member for Grey-Bruce has no point of privilege so far as the existence of this document is concerned. Tonight, the Postmaster General has admitted the existence of the document. He declares it has some different purpose than we might have thought, but he admits the existence of the document. He states, in his own words, what the purpose of it has been. I say that Mr. Speaker should reconsider this matter, if this document is now admitted by all concerned to exist, reconsideration should be given to the matter of whether or not it should be tabled, either by the member for Grey-Bruce, who has a copy of it, or preferably by the Postmaster General himself who has now admitted its existence.
The Postmaster General now comes under the citation in the book which says that a minister of the crown, having made a reference to a document, must produce it. The Postmaster General made a reference to the document. He has admitted its existence. He has made certain statements as to the use of that document, and therefore the rules of the house now require him to produce that document. I ask that Mr. Speaker reconsider this very serious matter that has arisen in the midst of this debate tonight.
At this juncture, I must say that I am not aware of having used certain words which were attributed to me by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, namely, and I quote:
We have been told by him we have to take the minister's word and that the hon. member for Grey-Bruce has no point of privilege so far as the existence of this document is concerned.
What I endeavoured to say was that the question was, in effect, a dispute between two members as to allegations of facts.
While I do not wish to enter into a debate on this question, it might be helpful if I were to review a few of the proceedings leading up to the incident of last evening.
On Wednesday, October 16, 1963, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) proposed a motion in the following terms, namely:
That an order of the house do issue for a list of "consultants" prepared in the office of the Postmaster General for the guidance of cabinet ministers and copies of all correspondence between ministers of the crown and the "consultants" in each riding.
Question of Privilege
Whereupon, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgili), as reported at page 3626 of Hansard, stated:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder could I raise a question of privilege with respect to this motion. I think Your Honour on reading it will see that the language of the motion is so obscure that it would not be possible for anyone reading the motion by itself- which is all that is before the house-to discern what the hon. gentleman was driving at. I have consulted the Postmaster General, who tells me that in his office no document of any description was prepared for the guidance of his colleagues, and therefore there could be no such document even if the motion were put.
Later on in the discussion the Postmaster General is recorded at page 3626 as having stated:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State should know whether he has received such a list for his guidance, but I never sent out any list for the guidance of the Secretary of State or any other minister. It does not exist. Therefore I do not think we should answer in regard to something that does not exist.
The following day, Thursday, October 17, 1963 the hon. member for Grey-Bruce, rising on a question of privilege, held in his hand a document which he alleged to be the document that the hon. member for Winnipeg North sought to obtain by virtue of his motion.
It is a fact, of course, that the Postmaster General acknowledges the existence of a document that is kept in his office, but he contends that the document is for his own personal use. I would refer hon. members to page 3884 of yesterday's Hansard.
I need not refer again at this time to the discussion which arose last evening, but it seems to me that the debate which occurred last night brings us back to our original point of departure. The problem, as I see it, is a matter of debate. On the one hand it is claimed that there is no such document as described in the terms of the motion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North while, on the other, it is contended that such document does exist, and the hon. member for Grey-Bruce exhibited a document in the house which he contends fits the terms of the motion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North.
It is not the duty of the Chair, nor is he in a position to decide whether or not there is such a document. If the matter is debated the Chair cannot and must not participate therein. I need only remind hon. members that in this regard standing order 10 reads in part as follows:
Mr. Speaker shall not take part in any debate before the house.
Before terminating my remarks I might refer to part of the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre wherein he states:

Question of Privilege
The Postmaster General now comes under the citation in the book which says that a minister of the crown, having made a reference to a document, must produce it.
At page 460, May's sixteenth edition, it is stated:
Another rule, or principle of debate, may be here added. A minister of the crown is not at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or other state paper not before the house, unless he be prepared to lay it on the table.
In Bourinot's fourth edition at page 337 it is stated:
It is a parliamentary rule that when a minister of the crown quotes a public document in the house, and founds upon it an argument or assertion, that document, if called for, ought to be produced.
At page 338 of the same publication it is stated in part as follows:
A minister who summarizes a correspondence but does not actually quote from it is not bound to lay it on the table.
The effect of the same rule is to be found in section 2 of citation 159, Beauchesne's fourth edition, wherein in part it is stated as follows:
2. A minister of the crown is not at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or other state paper not before the house, unless he be prepared to lay it upon the table.
There is, I suggest, a difference between referring to a document and the citing or reading from the same. Using these citations as my authority, it seems to me that the rule referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre does not apply in this instance.
In conclusion I should like to say that it is not within the competence of the Chair to order any minister to produce a document that may or may not be in his office. In this regard I refer hon. members to a ruling of the Chair and a decision of the house thereon, which is to be found at page 237 of the Journals, April 28, 1952.
In my opinion, there not being a prima facie case of privilege, I do not feel that the motion as moved by the hon. member for Yukon is in order.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: GREAT LAKES-ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROCLAMATION OF ACT AND NAMING OF TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise hon. members that the act to provide for the placing of the maritime transportation unions of Canada under the management and control of trustees has been proclaimed today.
The governor in council, Mr. Speaker, has established the membership of the board of trustees. The chairman of the board of trustees is to be Mr. Justice Victor Leonard Dryer of Vancouver, a member of the supreme court of the province of British Columbia.

Mr. Justice Dryer was created a Queen's Counsel in 1957. He was a member of the legal firm of Ellis, Dryer and McTaggart in the city of Vancouver. He was active for many years in labour relations, particularly representing unions in collective bargaining and conciliation work.
The second member of the board of trustees is Judge Rene Lippe, of the magistrate's court, Montreal. Judge Lippe has a wide reputation as an arbitrator, mediator and conciliator. He is a permanent arbitrator under certain collective agreements in the province of Quebec. Recently he was the mediator in the settlement of the longshoremen's strike in Montreal, and he has been appointed to investigate all trust funds being held for the benefit of longshoremen in Montreal, Quebec city, Three Rivers, Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick.
The third member of the board is Mr. Charles H. Millard of Toronto. Mr. Millard has been for many years associated with the united steel workers of America and served as Canadian congress of labour vice president for many years. As a representative of the Canadian congress of labour he played an important part in the development of international trade unionism following world war II, as an alternate member of the executive board of the international confederation of free trade unionism. He retired last year as director of organization for the international confederation of free trade unionism.
I am pleased to advise, Mr. Speaker, that all these gentlemen have agreed to accept these heavy responsibilities and will meet in Ottawa today to consider their future activities.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: GREAT LAKES-ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROCLAMATION OF ACT AND NAMING OF TRUSTEES
speechtext:
I know the house will welcome the announcement that has been made and the quality of the membership that composes the board of trustees. I would add that we in this parliament, without regard to party, will uphold the rule of law in this country and will join together to ensure that the laws passed by parliament, the representatives of the people, shall not be flouted or mocked by the cavalier actions of anyone, however powerful.
I want the house to know that this is our attitude. We have pressed the government for action for several weeks. They have found that when an immovable inertia meets an irresistible force the result is lawlessness and anarchy. The government has acted now, we say belatedly; but belatedly or not, this parliament is united.

subtopic: GREAT LAKES-ANNOUNCEMENT OF PROCLAMATION OF ACT AND NAMING OF TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government's action in proclaiming the trusteeship legislation and

appointing the trustees has not come a bit too soon. Last Monday evening I said that I for one was not prepared to criticize the government for the considerable time which it took in canvassing the possibility of a private trusteeship. But since that had apparently failed I felt then, as I feel now, that the government's record for decisiveness depended on what it did at this time. I am glad that the government has at last acted in this regard, because we have known since last Friday that the men have been ordered to walk off the ships. When I asked the Prime Minister the day before yesterday whether the government would consider setting up a government control over the shipping industry, he said, as reported at page 3815 of Hansard:
-I hope that the situation tomorrow will not require that kind of solution.
Well, "tomorrow" has come and gone and the situation is not better; it is worse. I think the government has not moved any too soon, because if it had delayed any longer the situation would have got entirely out of hand.
I think the trustees who have been appointed will commend themselves to most people in Canada. I am not familiar with the chairman, although I understand he has a good reputation. Judge Lippe is well known in the mediation of labour disputes; he has a good reputation and a good record of achievement. Mr. C. H. Millard, who has been absent from Canada for a number of years acting as world secretary of the international confederation of free trade unions, has gained a wide experience in the trade union movement throughout the free world, and I think he will bring to this task understanding and decisiveness.
But I want to say to the government that the personnel of this board, and their effectiveness, will now be dependant upon the support which they get from the government. They face a very difficult situation. Many of the S.I.U. locals have already taken votes not to return to their ships. This board of trustees will have to make some very difficult decisions. They will first of all have to separate the leadership of the S.I.U. from the membership. They will then have the task of trying to persuade the men to go back on the ships. If the men defy them I want to say to the government that we in this party will be asking the government to take the necessary steps to appoint a government controller over shipping so that this board of trustees is not left in an impossible situation.
I want to assure the government that any steps they take to re-establish shipping on the great lakes will have our support. We only hope they will neither drag their feet nor 28902-5-2484

Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to hear the statement made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) to the effect that the trusteeship has been proclaimed today and that the three trustees have taken up their duties.
We from the province of Quebec especially welcome the appointment of Mr. Justice Rene Lippe. We know him well since we had the privilege to see him at work during various labour disputes.
Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that all hon. members recognize now the importance of the task entrusted to these three trustees. In fact, this is an extremely delicate and difficult job, pregnant with responsibilities and consequences, considering the actions that these men will be called upon to take in order to settle the dispute within the labour unions, since this trusteeship that is being applied today constitutes a precedent which may likely recur in the future.
It is therefore essential that those three trustees be very careful in the way they carry out their duties. They will have to enforce the law in all fairness and try not to become a third dictatorship, because, according to an item published in a daily paper this morning, one of the seafarers who are at the basis of this conflict stated that when the men chose the dictatorship imposed by the union leader, they had the choice

External Affairs
between two dictatorships that of the Canada Steamship Lines or that of Hal Banks, and they chose the one who paid them most.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think that all hon. members in this house will have to keep a close watch so that this trusteeship does not become a third dictatorship, but rather a solution to this one problem.
I believe that we should also draw the attention of the trustees and of the house to the fact that those seamen are not the only guilty party, that they are not solely responsible for the present situation and that, if there has been a dictatorship of the shipping companies on the great lakes, this trusteeship will have to ensure that such company dictatorship does not repeat itself. Indeed, it will even have to take positive sanctions against the Canada Steamship Lines, which contributed to the dislocation of the existing order and tried to evade the law of this country.

speechtext:

subtopic: CRITERIA FOR DESIGNATED AREAS
speechtext:
1. Under the established criteria, a national employment service area qualifies as a designated development area provided:
(a)	it has been classified by the Department of Labour as a labour surplus area for one half or more of the summer months (May to October) during the past eight years; and it has experienced an employment increase of less than one half the national average over the same period; or
(b)	it has been classified by the Department of Labour as a labour surplus area for one third or more of the summer months (May

Questions
to October) during the past eight years; and it has experienced an employment decrease over the same period; or
(c)	it has been classified by the Department of Labour as a labour surplus area for one half or more of the summer months (May to October) during the past three years; and it has experienced an employment decrease in each one of the past three years.
(d)	However, an area shall not be designated if the average monthly national employment service registrations for the three months of May, June and July, expressed' as a percentage of the total number of paid workers in the area,
(i)	is less in the current year than in the preceding year and less in the preceding year than in the year preceding that year, and
(ii)	is less in the current year than in the year preceding the preceding year by at least 45 per cent and the area would not, if the three months of May, June and July in the current year were considered to be a single month, have been classified by the Department of Labour as a substantial labour surplus area for that month.
2.	Three tax incentives are proposed for designated development areas. These measures will become effective as soon as the necessary amendments to the Income Tax Act have been passed by parliament.
(a)	A taxpayer in computing income for income tax purposes will be allowed to exclude the income earned by a certified new manufacturing and processing enterprise during the period of 36 months after it commences operations. In order to qualify, a new business must begin commercial operations during the 24 month period following the date of enactment of the amendments to the Income Tax Act. The date of commencement of commercial operations will be certified by the Minister of Industry when he certifies a new business.
(b)	New machinery and equipment that would otherwise fall in class 8 of the income tax regulations, which is acquired for use in certified new manufacturing and processing enterprises, shall be eligible for accelerated capital cost allowances. A rate of 50 per cent on a straight line basis will be permitted on new machinery and equipment acquired in the 24 month period following the date of enactment of the amendments to the Income Tax Act. This compares with a normal rate of 20 per cent on the diminishing balance basis.
It will not be necessary for a taxpayer to take these accelerated allowances during his three year income tax exemption. They may be deferred and deducted after that period.
(c)	New buildings acquired in designated areas will qualify for accelerated capital cost
[Mr. MacEachen.l
allowances at the rate of 20 per cent per year on a straight line basis. This compares with a normal rate of 5 per cent on a diminishing balance basis for most buildings, or 10 per cent for buildings of frame or similar construction.
In order to qualify for this accelerated write-off, the new buildings must be acquired in the 24 month period which will apply for the other income tax incentives in the designated areas.
Under the municipal winter works program as applicable to designated areas, the government of Canada will reimburse each municipality in these areas 60 per cent of the direct payroll costs of approved projects which are incurred during the period November 1, 1963 to April 30, 1964.
The federal government has accelerated for the forthcoming winter those government construction projects which are located in these areas.
3.	Under the established criteria, no areas have qualified for designation in the provinces of Prince Edward Island, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia.

maintopic: SELLING PRICE OF BEET SUGAR PRODUCED IN WEST
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Justice, in view of the monstrous increase in the price of sugar, whether he is in a position to answer the question that I asked him yesterday relative to the sale of beet sugar produced at the refineries in Winnipeg and Lethbridge, which is selling at a price which takes into consideration the freight from Montreal to the places of production, rather than the freight rates from the places of production.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SELLING PRICE OF BEET SUGAR PRODUCED IN WEST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the answer to the question which the Leader of the Opposition asked yesterday. Perhaps I had better read into the record the question as he posed it then:
Mr. Speaker, as a supplementary question I would ask the minister whether in so far as western Canadian beet sugar is concerned which is refined at Winnipeg and Lethbridge, the people in western Canada are being penalized by having to pay the world sugar price, plus freight charges, as if the sugar was shipped from Montreal, when in fact it is coming from one or other of those two refineries.
The answer that has been given to me by the director of the combines investigation branch is as follows: Generally speaking, the refinery price of cane sugar in western Canada is equivalent to the Montreal or Vancouver price, whichever is the closer point, plus freight, the price of beet sugar being slightly lower. The director advises that such a situation can exist without there being any offence against the Combines Investigation Act.
As stated on a previous occasion, the increase in Canadian sugar prices is attributable to the increase in world raw sugar prices. Because of increasing world consumption and production difficulties there is unlikely to be any immediate improvement. Since the increase in refined sugar prices is a direct reflection of world market conditions over
Inquiries of the Ministry which Canada has no control, action under the Combines Investigation Act cannot be expected to correct the situation. The director is, however, continuing to keep the matter under close scrutiny, and should any aspect give him reason to believe that an offence against the act is being committed, he will take the action that the statute requires.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, October 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson (for the Secretary of State):
That a select committee be appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker the procedures and organization of this house, for the purpose of suggesting any changes that would assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business and would strengthen parliament and make it more effective; that the committee have power to send for persons and papers; that it report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house; and that it consist, in addition to Mr. Speaker, of 14 members to be designated at a later date.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall only require a very few minutes to complete my contribution to this debate, as I am sure the house is anxious to deal with this matter and get the committee set up so that it can go to work; and when the committee reports later on its activities we can debate its recommendations.
When I finished the other day I was talking of one change which might be useful, and that was to extend and make more effective the committee work of the house. Last January the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen) who was then in the opposition, when discussing this matter asked some questions which I think bear repetition because they do deal with this question in a very succinct and useful way. As reported on page 3284 of Hansard he said:
I ask myself whether there are Important changes which can be made in the rules of the house which would effect real economies in time. We have reduced the time on the address. Shall we reduce it two more days and thereby deny more

members the opportunity to take part? Shall we reduce the budget debate and thereby deny more members an opportunity to take part? Shall we reduce the number of supply motions and deny private members an opportunity to raise votes of non-confidence against the government? Shall we reduce the number of readings of a bill? Shall we have only one reading and pass the bill at one stage? This is the kind of important change which will have to be made in the rules in order to effect real economies.
I think, Mr. Speaker, he could also have asked another very pertinent question: Shall we do away with the resolution stage of a bill?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
The resolution stage had very great meaning in earlier years, particularly in the 18th and 17th centuries, but it does not seem to me to have the same kind of meaning today. It takes up a lot of time and results in a good deal of repetition of debate on a particular subject. Perhaps this is something which could be changed, though I agree that the committee would have to look into matters of that kind very carefully. While the committee can, and I am sure will, do a thorough job under your leadership, with the learned assistance which you, Mr. Speaker, will receive, perhaps there are things which we can do at once by agreement of the house after discussion among the leaders of the various parties. Perhaps there are things we can do now while the committee is at work- and it may take many weeks, indeed months, to complete its work-which will increase the effectiveness of this house during this particular session.
This subject was discussed a year ago, in November and December of 1962 and January 1963, during the previous parliament. I remember speaking in that debate in respect to the proposals which were made at that time to speed up the work of the session, proposals which incidentally did not come to anything. Perhaps these might be revived now, and after discussion with the leaders of the parties we could put them into effect immediately. I said, as reported at page 2835 of Hansard for December 19, 1962:
We have agreedand by "we" I meant our own party which was then in opposition, and other opposition parties-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext: No, that is not right.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
All right, I will refer to our own party. We discussed this matter with other opposition parties at the time, and with my hon. friend too; but I will restrict my observations to my own party. I said:
We have agreed to the allocation of time to specific legislation. That would be done by agreement, and it is a very important concession for an opposition to make.

This would mean, Mr. Speaker, that by agreement-and this is done regularly in Westminster-we would allocate a certain number of days considered appropriate for each piece of legislation to that legislation, and at the end of the agreed allocation of time the vote would then be taken on the various stages of the legislation. We on our side, when we were in opposition last year, agreed to that. Then I went on:
We have agreed to a reduction, if it is a reduction, to 30 minutes of the time spent on orai questions on orders of the day-
Speaking on this same matter a few weeks before, a very distinguished member of the government of that time had this to say, as reported on page 2011 of Hansard for November 26, 1962:
I think that the number of these questions could be greatly reduced: and if we were also to have a self-denying ordinance that, under ordinary circumstances, we would not go over half an hour on questions before orders of the day we would save 15 full days in an ordinary session without, as I see it, losing any ground that might be gained through questions or in any way interfering with the rights of the opposition.
That was the position taken at that time, Mr. Speaker, by the right hon. gentleman who was then prime minister and who is now Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). There is something else which by agreement we could surely consider at once, because I believe a year ago we had come to virtual agreement on it.
Then a third proposal which we put forward, with which we in the official opposition were in agreement at that time, was this. I said in my remarks on December 19, 1962, as reported at page 2835 of Hansard:
We have agreed to the prolongation of each day's sitting beyond ten o'clock if that should be necessary to complete the current business before the house or the committee of the whole.
These were three specific suggestions put forward at that time and given a great deal of consideration by the other parties. They were proposals which would have resulted in increasing the effectiveness of the work of the house; and I would hope that while this committee is going into this matter in depth perhaps we could agree to those three proposals which were discussed last year. We could agree to them at once and, perhaps, discussions could be held without delay for that purpose.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister state to the house why those proposals were not accepted by the house as a whole? They were acceptable to the government.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
