I am speaking for this party, which was the official opposition at the time.
Procedure Committee
We accepted those proposals. I am well aware of the circumstances surrounding the situation, but I think it would be better to let the leaders of other parties speak as to their own attitude. I believe it is more important to see whether we can reach agreement on this matter now than to worry about why we were not able to reach agreement on it a year ago.
I commend this resolution in the hope that the committee will be set up and that its findings will be acted upon as soon as possible. May I also express the hope that we can, pending the report of this committee, agree on certain measures which will speed up our work and make the House of Commons more effective.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
I agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) that everything possible should be done to bring about efficiency of operation and the expedition of business, provided the inherent rights of parliament are not interfered with. The right hon. gentleman spoke the other night of the cynicism toward parliament which finds expression through various persons outside the House of Commons. They speak of parliament as a place where work is not done and where wrangling takes place. They often claim that business, if it operated in the same way, would not be very successful.
Well, we have had a number of businessmen come into parliament in recent days and weeks and they have found that the methods of business are not entirely in keeping with the deliberative nature of parliament. I have not anybody in mind at the moment, but I feel sure there is one or another among those sitting opposite who would entirely agree that the expressions uttered by him or them before coming into parliament have been greatly diminished, in the light of experience, and with a greater knowledge of the operations of parliament and its traditions than could be gained outside this chamber.
I believe, with the Prime Minister, that the parliamentary machinery needs to be examined from time to time and that we must make parliament effective, for a parliament which is not effective can lead to the establishment of dictatorship as an alternative. Parliament is judged by the way in which it transacts business. Again, I say that expedition and efficiency are important. At the same time, there must be no sacrifice of the essential rights of parliament. What I intend to do is to refer in general to some suggestions and ideas which have come to me during the years. I think that on three occasions when I was prime minister we brought before the house a motion to set up a committee such as this. There was a fourth occasion when

Procedure Committee
one of the members of the Social Credit group did the same. Parliament today includes a number of members who sat on those committees. There was a surprising degree of unanimity that something should be done. Changes were made as recommended. Other suggested changes were not put into effect.
When I read all the criticisms of parliament, my view, after many years of membership here, is that while parliament has shortcomings, without it there cannot be freedom. To overcome these shortcomings while remaining a bulwark of freedom, parliament must constantly change in order to meet changing conditions, at the same time remaining changeless in its basic concepts and traditions. The Prime Minister dealt with the old days of parliament, with the beginnings of parliament. There has been bitterness in debate in parliament in every generation. The traditions of parliament carry us back four or five hundred years. The space between the Prime Minister and myself, as everyone knows, is that distance which will allow our sword points to touch; beyond that we can go no further. We do not carry swords any more. We use, on occasion, rapiers of debate which do not require this distance between us. But the tradition remains.
I, for years, have felt that to raise the debating strength of parliament one of the first things we might do is to remove these desks. In the mother of parliaments, debate is much more effective, because of the difficulty of finding a place on which to lay one's notes, than it can ever be in a place where all of us have before us our notes or supporting material. I read of Salisbury, Disraeli, Gladstone and Asquith who were able to speak almost interminably without notes. It was said of Balfour that most of his great speeches found their entire outline on the back of an envelope. Again, we must realize that they spoke in days when there was not that complexity, that variety in affairs, which denies anyone today the possibility of fully absorbing all the information necessary to discuss these various matters and to deliver speeches thereon with few notes.
I had that in mind-the removal of the desks. I will be frank and tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the idea was not very popular among some of those within my own party. A member once said to me, "If you do that, who is going to speak?" The same applies to members in all parts of the house. However, if we were to bring about this change, which I found myself unable to do, I think we would establish the number one prerequisite to a great House of Commons. The result would be shorter but more effective speeches.

In the old days the members of this house used to make long speeches. One has just to look at the debates of the House of Commons in 1885 on the Riel rebellion to realize how long speeches were in those days. I think the first four or five speeches were four or five hours each. Sir John felt he could summarize the whole matter in four hours. Those were the days of long speeches and short parliaments.
What are some of the suggestions that I should like to place before the house? The Prime Minister has mentioned the question of committees. I believe in committees, but experience has proven to me that if we endeavour to place controversial matters before committees they are not effective. Committees operate well in the field of external affairs. The public accounts committee has worked out very well. My suggestion brought about a change whereby you, Mr. Speaker, became chairman of that committee and whereby today the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) is chairman of that committee. But I have seen many other committees operate in which questions of a controversial nature were being discussed and which emasculated those committees and made them ineffective.
What are some of the suggestions that might be followed? One that has been made before concerns research facilities. There is not available to any member of parliament, except those on the treasury benches, the research facilities that should be available to all members. How to bring this about is a difficult question. We cannot communicate with the civil service. To do so would be unfair to them. It would place them in an impossible position. But I think one matter that should be studied carefully is how to bring about in connection with the House of Commons a group of research officials that would be available to all members.
Mention was made by the Prime Minister of the limitation of question time. When I first entered the House of Commons Mr. King was prime minister, and if there were more than one or two questions we thought that bedlam had broken loose. From about 1949 on the number of questions has gradually increased. When we were in government the number increased to an extent beyond anything that had been seen before. Today a similar situation prevails. Provided the answers given by the government are not evasive, provided they place the facts before us, provided they do not hide and cover up, as was alleged today and last night, I would be inclined to believe that if, in addition to the regular questions on the order paper, we all agreed to the self-denying ordinance to which the Prime Minister made reference, oral questions

could very well be limited considerably. To what extent would be a matter for determination and recommendation by the committee. In the United Kingdom the period is an hour and that covers written as well as oral questions.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext: And it is not every day.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
As the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) says, it is not every day. Speaking from recollection, I believe it is four days in the week. But when ministers start to hide and conceal and fail to reveal the true facts a private member in the United Kingdom then has the right to give 12 hours notice that there shall not be adjournment at ten o'clock but that he shall be able to bring before the house his cause of complaint. This is a very effective method. If it were introduced here I think it would be very helpful because it would assure that if the opposition was restricted in its questions it would be able to place before the house and the country the failure of the government, should it fail, to give proper answers.
I picked up at random Hansard of the British House of Commons for July 10, 1963. The house was ready to adjourn at 9.55 p.m. Mr. Patrick Wall, the member for Haltem-price, placed his views before the house and, having done so, the house finally adjourned at 29 minutes past ten o'clock. While the time during which questions can be asked in the British House of Commons is restricted, when the answers are not in keeping with the facts or for any other reason a member may move, and the motion is always accepted, that the house do not adjourn this evening at ten o'clock.
I come now to another matter raised by the Prime Minister, the question of whether or not there should be a debate at the resolution stage. I believe there should be and that it should be continued. There are some pieces of legislation where it is not necessary. There are others where suggestions, recommendations or criticisms made in the house cause the government to change its viewpoint. We have had a number of examples of that during the present session to which I am not going to allude at the moment. But it was as a result of the opposition's stand in the debate on the resolution stage, which some people called obstruction, that the great plans of the government were changed.
As far as the speech from the throne and budget debates are concerned I sometimes think that we take more time than is necessary on them. There used to be unlimited time, and when there was unlimited time for discussion on this matter parliament took little more time than it takes today with the
Procedure Committee
present limitation because, sir, as soon as you impose a limitation as a maximum that limitation tends to become the minimum.
In the days when the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Cardiff) first came into the house, we had the right to speak at great length. We had 40 minutes; but as the minutes were reduced the time for debate continued to be as long as previously. People spoke at shorter length, but if today an hon. member having the opportunity to speak for 40 minutes speaks for only 20 minutes everybody wonders why he did not use up his time. This is one of the effects of placing limitations on speeches.
Something else which has brought about the interminable length of discussion is the multiplication of parties. They all want their say, and it is much easier to arrive at rules to bring about expedition in parliament when there are two parties than when there are four and a half, or five.
What about supply motions? We fixed the time for two days on supply motions and used those two days on practically every occasion. I have often felt that if we were going to have six supply motions in a session it might be well to reduce the time to one day for five of them, with two days devoted to the first. I also feel that we could make a change whereby the government would move supply immediately after the speech from the throne, and have a two day debate at that time so that the estimates of various departments could come before the house, and so that we could put our teeth into something immediately without unnecessary delay.
What about the votes? Well, if there ever was anything more wasteful than the way in which we register a vote I do not know what it is. The other evening we waited and waited for an hon. member who apparently was having dinner or something. I am not going to identify him but we waited a long time for him. He represents a small party that has shown a pathological adherence to supporting the present government. The house was kept waiting for him, and this has happened on other occasions.
I do not suggest the introduction of mechanical devices. I have seen them in operation. We are in the age of automation, but I dislike seeing some of these pushbutton appliances whereby red or blue colours are shown when a vote is registered. I do not know what the disposition of colours would be for the parties to my left, what they would be in this present spectrum, but that is the way these appliances operate.
However, we waste 15 or 20 minutes waiting until hon. members are brought into the chamber. Why should we not be able to vote at 8.15 o'clock instead of waiting until almost

Procedure Committee
8.45 as we did last evening? Mr. Speaker, do you realize how long it takes for a vote in the United Kingdom parliament? The time taken is about two minutes. Members either go into one lobby or another and the speaker designates two tellers. It takes three minutes at the outside, and I ask why not make that change?
One year we had some 60 votes. Multiply 60 by 12 minutes and you have several days that are used up in voting. This is something that will not detract in any way from the dignity of the house. The British parliament introduced it in 1906 and there has never been any question about it since. I might read from May's Parliamentary Practice on this subject:
The present method of taking divisions in the House of Commons was introduced experimentally in session 1906... On a division being called the speaker or the chairman, as the case may be, gives the order "clear the lobby", and the tellers' doors in both lobbies are locked. After the lapse of two minutes from this direction the speaker or chairman again puts the question, and the ayes and noes respectively declare themselves.
There, sir, is something simple but effective in saving time without interfering in any way with the dignity of this chamber. I have seen nothing undignified in a member standing, being identified by the teller and then by the clerk, and finally the totalization being placed before you.
There is also the question of the working hours of the house. We extended the hours recently, but I see no reason that we should not be sitting longer hours right from the beginning of the session. I know the difficulties of the government and I know the load that rests on the Prime Minister's shoulders is very great. But in the British House of Commons the prime minister does not come into the house every day. When questions are asked he is there for the questions asked of him. He answers those questions and he leaves. There is no reason today that a man occupying the position of prime minister-except when'there is a controversial matter before the house-should be here and be required to stay throughout the period of orders of the day.
There is a change that could be made by altering the present system for questions. In the British house the government is never taken by surprise. The questions appear in numbered form on the order paper, and when it comes to No. 40 the questions to the Prime Minister appear. The only oral questions are the supplementary ones. I think our whole question period and the manner or carrying it on should be considered in detail and some recommendation made.
Then there is the organization of business. How often I remember hearing the Secretary
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
of State speaking about organization, with the knowledge he gained from being in the gallery as secretary to a prime minister, not as the grey eminence but as an eminence behind the prime minister. He used to ask, "Why don't you organize? What is wrong here?" He said to us, "Why don't you get along with the business?" He is not saying that any more, because he is the organizer and has found that the difficulties with the rules make it impossible for him to proceed with that sense of direction and certainty, qualities that were his when in opposition. I have often thought that the orderly dispatch of business would be more effective if a matter was brought before the house and proceeded with until concluded. If that rule were in effect, it would have played havoc with the pensions scheme; it would have played havoc with the Canada development plan. Both these measures seem to have become covered with weeds, weeds of uncertainty.
I mentioned the question of the estimates, in passing. I think that one of our responsibilities is to carefully examine and scrutinize the estimates. That is not done today; the important estimates are not brought in until near the end of the session. There is the Department of Agriculture. That is a very important department. All of us are looking forward with anticipation to hearing the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) let us in on the secrets of his department. He has been denied that opportunity. And so I could go on. This and other important departments have not been touched. In connection with the question of estimates, I think we have possibly gone too far in the matter of debating the individual items. If the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were called and hon. members could say they wanted to deal with this, that or the other phase of those estimates, I think we would save a great deal of time. In the United Kingdom their debates on the estimates are effective, but they are not concerned with the individual item, excepting in so far as it is a matter of particular attention.
Many of the estimates, those which concern non-contentious departments, could be sent to a committee for study. We have found how this system operates in fields that are non-controversial. I read criticism in the press with regard to obstruction. That has always been charged. When we sat on the other side of the chamber we contended- and at the moment I am being far from partisan-that we were being obstructed. Today those occupying the government benches say the same thing. But, sir, is it obstruction to stand firmly against something

that you believe to be wrong? If it had not been for the stand of this opposition would the 30 per cent securities tax not have been continued? We saw it was wrong, and we said so. If it had not been for the opposition, would there not be today an 11 per cent sales tax on building materials and production machinery? If there had not been an opposition would the old age pensioners be getting the $10 extra at this time that was promised them? The government always contend that any argument against their policies represents obstruction.
I look at the order paper. Mention was made of this matter today by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I ask hon. members to look at this order paper. What are we obstructing? What is the government's program? Where is it? Well, there are 27 items here. There are only one or two measures on this order paper that require early attention. The first item on the order paper is the surcharge measure. Then there is the bill to amend the Northwest Territories Act, and the bill respecting the Nunassiaq territory. There is the measure to repeal the Newfoundland Savings Bank Act; that is No. 4. The fifth item concerns public harbours in Ontario; the sixth concerns the Bankruptcy Act; the seventh has to do with the Income Tax Act. We are all paying this income tax, but the bill has not yet been passed.
Then there is the bill to amend the National Harbours Board Act, and that concerning the Carriage by Air Act. There are eight items in a row that, with the exception of the income tax measure, are not by any stretch of the imagination matters that are part and parcel of the government's plan. Next is the Department of Agriculture, the division into east and west. When we watch the Minister of Agriculture in action we wonder why they want to divide him up. Then there is the measure with respect to the Canadian National Railway Company; then the measure to further Canadian participation in the development of industries and undertakings in Canada and development of our resources and industries. This measure is also concerned with the setting up of the Canada Development Corporation. That seems to be one of those things that was thought of, written of and now, when it is to be brought to the House of Commons, this troubled government finds it will have to be changed.
The measure to amend the National Housing Act is of some importance. Then there is the resolution concerning the setting up of a joint committee to inquire into the question of consumer credit. There is the matter concerning the setting up of the committee on
Procedure Committee
railways, air lines and shipping. Mr. Speaker, that is No. 15. No. 16 is the measure to establish the Canada pension plan, which was born in hope and died in despair. They failed to obtain the agreement of the provinces and it now seems to belong to the ages.
One could go through the remainder of the items on the order paper. There is the measure to amend the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act in order that the authority may borrow additional money. Nobody is going to discuss that item at length. There is also the resolution in regard to grants to be made from the railway grade crossing fund. There is the measure to pay a salary not exceeding $400 a year to a surrogate judge in admiralty. These are not important matters. There is one exception: The measure in respect of the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act is important. There are only four pieces of legislation in that whole list which are of importance, and if they were brought before the house I am sure there would be general agreement in support of those principles.
The organization of the house is what is necessary, as the hon. gentleman has said on so many occasions. I read in the press about the obstructive tactics of parliament. I mentioned the other day something that I hope hon. members will take the trouble to look into. I refer to the debates in the Canadian House of Commons in 1912 and 1913. I would ask hon. members to first read what Sir Robert Borden said in his memoirs at pages 411 to 420. The debate began on January 14. They apparently went on day and night and the debate dragged on until February 27, when a motion was made that the bill be not proceeded with until after redistribution. Read what Sir Robert Borden writes. These were the great days, remember; the days of Borden and Laurier, when parliament was so effective. What happened?
Sir Robert goes on to say:
-at midnight Sir Wilfrid asked for adjournment and I asked for progress. At one a.m. I again asked progress and he asked adjournment. At two a.m. he moved a dilatory amendment. At 3.45 a.m., I went home leaving the opposing forces in line of battle: and I returned at 9.45 a.m.
Those were the great days of parliament. Today, we are criticized for not being in the house. Well, in those days the debate went on night and day until Saturday, March 8, at two o'clock in the morning.
Then, Sir Robert says this:
Members on each side were divided into three relays or shifts and were on duty for eight hours at a time. We had to adopt unusual precautions because we did not know at what hour the opposition might spring division and have a majority concealed and available.

Procedure Committee
Sometimes when I look over at my hon. friends opposite, I watch the Secretary of State as he goes through the counting process. Sometimes when he comes over to this side of the house I suspect that he is looking around to see whether or not the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) and those associated with him are still here.
I return to what Sir Robert has to say:
On Monday March 10 I held caucus-
On Friday, March 14, and again on the following day the debate became so violent as to occasion apprehension of personal conflict.
I am just reading the account of one debate. Those were the days when the debate was so bitter that there was danger of violent personal conflict. Then, he said:
After two hours' sleep. I had returned to the house on Friday afternoon. As midnight approached the Speaker twice had to take the chair amid scenes of great disorder.
The point I am making is this: People talk about obstruction now, but there was no criticism in those days when strong men took strong action. Finally, he says that things quietened down after he spoke briefly in French. I am sure if the right hon. Prime Minister or I ever tried that we would not have the same soporific effect. I continue to quote:
Considering in retrospect these weeks, the most strenuous and remarkable that have ever occurred in Canadian parliamentary history, I am satisfied that it was a mistake to carry out our tactics during the second week-
During that week the nerves of members on both sides were so frayed by excitement, strain and exhaustion that they lost in great measure their usual self-control.
This was parliament in the great days of Canadian parliamentary history. Then, he says that he went over to Sir Wilfrid, who was very angry, and Sir Wilfrid stated that he would give consideration to his request. Later on, Sir Wilfrid told him he was not prepared to make any arrangements. Sir Robert says:
I became greatly exhausted by the intense strain of the long debate, the night hours and the tumultuous scenes-
As was anticipated, Sir Wilfrid became violently enraged and his rage was shared by all his followers who made loud demonstrations.
Sir, when there are issues that divide us there must be nothing to restrict the freedom of debate. Furthermore, and this is as true today as it was when it was stated by Bagehot, the lack of great issues means the multiplicity of parties. In other words, when we have a great issue on which to fight we tend to coalesce. In those days to which I have been referring, this parliament stood out in its greatness and in some of the tumultuous scenes that are sometimes seen today.

I hope, sir, that we will be able to bring about changes in the rules. The failure of parliament to discharge its duty leads to contempt of parliament and parliamentarians. Without prestige you cannot discharge your responsibility. In those days, if any person were to flout parliament he was brought before the bar. In 1906, 1911 and 1912 the supreme court of parliament punished those who treated it with contempt and refused to follow the supreme laws that it had passed. The great danger in making too many changes in the rules is that this brings about a condition of affairs whereby the cabinet becomes even more powerful than it has been. The trend has been in the last 35 or 40 years for the cabinet to become all-powerful.
In the United Kingdom Lord Home assumed the prime ministership the other day and was the 45th prime minister since Walpole. However, the changes that have taken place since the last five prime ministers have held office have completely altered parliament. More and more the private member of parliament is of less and less importance. More and more the prime minister and the cabinet become all powerful. It is for this reason, as private members of parliament, we have to guard against too great changes in the rules. If there are too great changes, we may very well deprive the private member of rights of which he ought not to divest himself.
What we want to assure in parliament, as I see it, is that in debate we will provide the people with the information and facts. Only when the people know the facts can parliament properly operate. No matter what is said in parliament, unless it is given publicity either in the press, T.V. or radio, it is ineffective. The strength of the British parliament has been that the views of both sides, government and opposition, have received attention in the press. In other words, in order to stimulate interest and to maintain parliament, there must be the widest dissemination of news. I picked up a copy of the London Times when I was in my office and noticed something which I think is important. This is a July issue when parliament was sitting. This is the way parliament and its activities are described in the British press. There is a reference to the house of lords; then, the questions in the house of commons. Over here is the back bench and miscellany; "Macmillan brings M.P.s news from Moscow." There is almost three quarters of a page dealing with each and every member who participated in debate, thus enabling the people to have the facts. These are the elements that make for a strong parliament and give members a desire to bring up the things that they have in mind.

The important things are the ability to cooperate amongst ourselves; the ability to cooperate with the government on the things in which we all agree and to disagree strongly when we do disagree. Above all, the people as a whole should be provided with information as to what is happening in the house. The people should be given the story of parliament as it is. There is nothing more distressing to a new member of parliament, or even a backbench member who has spent time preparing a speech, than to find that, having worked on it for days and having made a study of the subject, he does not get any reference in the press. On the other hand, if the same member were to use language which was unparliamentary he would then be assured of publicity.
What I have said this afternoon has simply been a desire to indicate that we of the opposition, and I as Leader of the Opposition, want to co-operate to the fullest extent possible with the government and leaders of the other parties in bringing about in this house rules that will make parliament more effective than it has ever been before.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the New Democratic party have already indicated their willingness to pass this motion setting up the parliamentary committee, either without any debate at all or with a restricted debate. We believe that the main discussion should take place in the committee and that we should get the matter to the committee just as quickly as possible. Therefore, unless the debate is an extended one we certainly will not be doing anything which will protract discussion on this motion.
However, I want to make a few observations. The New Democratic party believes that far reaching changes are necessary in parliament's methods of conducting the business affairs of this country. The reputation and functioning of parliament are in doubt. We ought to be frank and face the fact that there is growing criticism of parliament, some of it unjustified but most of it deserved. Parliamentary democracy is on trial today, and hardly a month goes by but that we read of some country in which democratic parliamentary institutions have been swept aside and replaced by a dictatorship of one form or another. If parliament is to survive as an institution it must be able to adapt itself to the pace and complexities of this modern age.
There is no doubt about the need for streamlining parliamentary procedures. There are more decisions to be made today and there is less time in which to make them. Communications have so improved in our modern society that the public is better able to assess
28902-5-250
Procedure Committee
what parliament is doing and whether or not it is doing an effective job. The public are demanding more efficiency in the conduct of business and they are asking for speedier processes in the reaching of decisions. It is true that parliament is a forum for the discussion of public affairs, but we should not lose sight of the fact that it is also a workshop where the country's housekeeping business is done.
The point we want to stress, a point which we hope the committee will keep in mind, is that this question which we are referring to them is not something for experts alone. In the past we have tended to look upon parliamentary procedure as the sole prerogative of insiders who are steeped in legal precedents and historical practices. We believe we have to bring this whole subject out into the arena of public debate and take a fresh look at the role of parliament. The mere reshuffling of the rules is not enough; the role and function of parliament itself needs to be examined. I hope that when the committee is set up it will call witnesses, bring in some of the professors of political science across Canada and people who have made a study of parliamentary government, so that it can take a broad look at this question and not merely spend its time tinkering with a few of the rules.
I am sorely tempted, Mr. Speaker, as must be every other hon. member who speaks in this debate, to suggest changes which the house ought to make in its procedures, such as sending more departmental estimates to committees, appointing a permanent speaker, a daily roll call of members, a reorganization of the question period, the elimination of the resolution stage in introducing bills, and empowering committees to sit between sessions of parliament. All of these are things one might like to discuss and elaborate. But that is not the purpose of this debate; it is the function of the committee to look at matters such as that, and to discuss them.
There is one thing the committee might consider, and it is that one or two of these more self-evident changes could be submitted back to the house in an interim report, on which the house could act fairly soon, the broader question being left to the committee to report on in its final report. The purpose of this debate, as I see it, should be to state guide lines for the committee, not to start doing their work for them. I think we should be suggesting to the committee the need for a reorganization and a re-examination of parliament's basic functions in an age of speed, in such a way that parliament can best serve the needs of a complex and industrial interdependent society.

Procedure Committee
It seems to me that if we are going to have this re-examination of parliament's basic role in our democracy, there are two factors we should keep in mind. The first factor is that there is today a greater complexity in the conduct of public affairs. Government now touches people's lives at more points, and government decisions are of greater concern to the average citizen than they were 50 or 75 years ago. Because parliament is not geared to deal with this complex interdependent society, the tendency has been to vest more and more power in the hands of the cabinet, and especially in the hands of the prime minister. Consequently, there is a real danger that parliament will become a mere rubber stamp the function of which will be to debate cabinet decisions, with no role whatsoever in the decision making process itself. I think this is the reason why so many members become frustrated and impatient. I think the average private member wants a role which is more meaningful than merely pounding his desk for the Prime Minister or the Leader of the Opposition when they engage in verbal fireworks.
Not only must we look at the role of parliament in this complex society, but I hope the committee will give some thought to evolving an effective role for the private member both on the government side and on the opposition side. As I see it the opposition is not elected just to oppose; that to me is an invalid proposition. I think opposition members have a responsibility to scrutinize all public expenditure, to offer alternative proposals and to put forward new ideas for consideration by the government. To do this, they must have information and they must have access to vital material through appropriate parliamentary committees. If they do not get this information, the opposition has no function other than one of tawdry deviousness or petulant needling combined with shrill partisanship, which tends to emphasize points of difference rather than areas of agreement. Secrecy always leads to mistrust. The best way to remove suspicion is to give the private member the right to be informed.
I think government members need to have a more effective role to play. They should not be looked upon just as a voting bloc to approve cabinet decisions and force them through the house. We need to devise methods by which members on the government side have a part to play in the decision-making process itself. In this as in every parliament, a great deal of talent is going to waste, particularly on the government side, because opposition members can, of course, use their time asking questions and doing a great many other things. I think we need to devise a parliamentary system which would loosen

the reins of cabinet control and give private members a more effective part to play. This will not be done by merely changing a few rules in the rule book. We need a new concept of the role of the private member in a democratic institution.
Having said this, I agree readily that in the final analysis the successful operation of parliament must depend on the sense of responsibility which is exercised by individual members. No amount of alteration of the rules will improve the situation unless we have a government and an opposition which are determined to make parliament an effective instrument. If we have a government which is indecisive or autocratic, on the one hand, or an opposition that is obstructive and irresponsible on the other, then certainly parliament will lose the respect of the public. The final appeal to all of us must be to put parliament before party and to put democracy before partisanship.
The house is giving to this committee a heavy responsibility at a time when democracy is undergoing careful scrutiny and examination. As far as we in the New Democratic party are concerned we assure its members of our co-operation as they seek to make parliament a more effective instrument of the people's will.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
May I
say on behalf of the Social Credit party that we readily lend our support to the motion to set up this committee. We think it should come into being with a minimum of debate or, if possible, without any further debate, because I believe it is the responsibility of the committee to make the recommendations which all agree are so urgently needed.
The events in parliament this session, even those of today and last night, as well as of the last few days, show clearly enough how greatly a complete overhaul of procedure is needed. In the wisdom of hindsight, I sometimes wish the Glassco commission had been asked to take a look, even if in confidence, at the workings of this body of which we are all members. There is much criticism today throughout Canada regarding the functioning of parliament. Some of us may say it is not justified. Some of us might say the press has overemphasized certain aspects. But I believe there is no way whatsoever in which we can justify some of the things which take place in this house. I was shocked when I picked up a copy of the Ottawa Citizen of October 8 and read that 13-year-olds who had visited this house were ashamed of the antics in the Commons and had stated the reasons for their opinion. At about the same time Toronto newspapers carried a condensation of editorials which

had appeared across Canada on this subject. Invariably these editorials called attention to examples of the gross inadequacy and inefficiency of our operations here. This is the image of parliament that is being put before the people. Certainly, people living in a democratic society such as we have in Canada ought to have much more reason to take pride in the institution of parliament.
The Prime Minister mentioned this afternoon that there might be some things with regard to which we could take immediate action, if agreement could be reached among the various groups in the house pending the report of the committee. I think that is a positive suggestion and we would be happy to co-operate in any possible way in which this could be done. The Leader of the Opposition spoke about the preservation of freedom as it relates to the basic rules of parliamentary procedure. I suggest that a few changes which would help parliament to function more effectively will not destroy the freedom which, we all agree, centres on a democratic House of Commons such as this is. On the contrary, they will strengthen it. We must not deceive ourselves by allowing ourselves to become encrusted with the attitude which develops through spending long hours in this building, forgetting what the people outside are thinking.
It seems to me that much of what goes on here is done with a desire to play to the galleries, in the hope that someone will get a headline, instead of working toward the objective, which should be our responsibility, of getting the work done which we have been sent here to do. It is therefore imperative that we arrive at some basic reforms in our procedure. I agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) that it is not just a few alterations to the rules which are needed, but a complete overhaul in order to adjust the functioning of this house to the times in which we live. The improvement in communications alone makes the situation today entirely different from the situation which existed in the days when many of these rules and regulations under which we now operate were formulated.
One of the dangers we face is that the bigger and bigger schemes which the government is continually introducing cannot be adequately supervised, because the supervisory machinery of parliament is becoming so overloaded that it is breaking down. That is one good argument in favour of a private enterprise society. We should all keep this consideration in mind as new plans are introduced for still more far reaching activities on the part of the federal government.
28902-5-250J
Procedure Committee
We, as a house, now cost the country more money than we did twelve months ago. The cost of our wasting time is correspondingly higher. Therefore we have the added responsibility to make sure that we do provide at least some measure of efficiency. The rules of procedure in this house have often been compared with the rules of driving. Let us remember it is not simply good rules that are necessary but good drivers. In our case it is good parliamentarians. Everyone notices the bad driver, just as they do the politician who makes the most noise. The good driver and the good parliamentarian, I believe, is usually the man who gets on with the job without attracting too much attention or causing annoyance to his fellows. In this regard it is important that we remember the human element. We must also remember that it is the welfare of our own citizens and not the political parties to which we belong that we are paid to represent in the House of Commons.
I am not as experienced with the functionings of parliament as many members of the house are, but it has been my privilege to visit, observe and study the functioning of democratic parliaments in many different countries. It has even been my privilege to sit on committees that have been responsible for the setting up of parliaments initially in some countries where parliaments in the democratic sense of the word had not been known before.
Just recently I have been to New Zealand and Australia and I should like to share with the house some of the things I observed there, in order to show that other legislative houses pledged to the same freedom and the same type of democratic, parliamentary government that we are, have met some of these problems ahead of us, and as a result are much more effective and efficient in what they are doing.
In New Zealand, for example, there are no Monday sittings at all. There are 23 hours of sittings a week extending between Tuesday afternoon and Friday afternoon. In New Zealand the question period is limited to 30 minutes and unanswered questions have precedence the following day. An urgent question for oral answer must be submitted in writing to the minister concerned and to the Speaker, and it is in the Speaker's discretion whether he allows it to be asked. The last 30 minutes of each sitting day are taken up with a debate on the adjournment with speeches limited to five minutes in order that half a dozen speakers may have an opportunity to participate in winding up the debate. The normal length of speeches allowed to any individual member is 20 minutes. Division

Procedure Committee
bells are rung for only three minutes. Only three speeches are allowed to a member in committee, the lengths of time of those speeches being 10 minutes, 5 minutes and 5 minutes. Except immediately following the budget, the government has the right to go into committee of supply without a debate. These are a few points that were very interesting to me as I watched the New Zealand house functioning.
In Australia the situation is a little different, but they also have solved many of their problems long before we have. Because of distances in Australia being comparable to ours, their situation may be somewhat more applicable. In Australia the problem about which we have been concerned here for the last several weeks, regarding the seating arrangements in the house and what constitutes a party, would never have arisen because they have a few simple regulations that spell out, a, b, and c, what constitutes a party and what constitutes the order of precedence in the house. There would have been no argument at all.
In Australia I was impressed that the house there sits only from Tuesday morning until Friday noon. The objective is to put the member of parliament back in direct contact with his constituents as much as possible. Their house only sits three weeks out of every four. You may say that this does not give them much time to get their work on legislation done, but their hours of sitting and their rules are such that I believe they get as much done in three and a half days a week and three weeks per month, as we do.
This arrangement permits cabinet ministers to catch up on the administration of their departments. It permits the government to plan its policies. These are the reasons as they were explained to me. It permits cabinet ministers to visit the country and to keep in touch with their own administration. It permits the members of parliament to do their work at the constituency level. Most of all, it permits the members of parliament and senators to find out what public opinion is and what their own constituents are expecting them to do. Members are allowed travel and telephone connection back and forth with their constituencies. Furthermore, their rules place the member's main responsibility to his constituency, and the government supplies a constituency office for every member. That is where the member's permanent secretary is.
I was interested to hear the remarks of the leader of the official opposition with regard to benches. Neither the New Zealand nor the Australian parliaments have desks like we have. They are debating forums and because of that I think they are much more

realistically effective. I had originally disagreed with this idea until I actually watched these two parliaments functioning with no desks, in the same way as does the mother of parliaments. Having had some experience in this house I became convinced that this was a good idea.
Those are some of the ways in which these countries have met these problems. Australia has a controlled question hour and their regulations are quite similar to those in New Zealand. In addition, they have a permanent voters' list and as a result every person, whether he happens to be in hospital or in the foreign service in some other part of the world or in some other part of the country at election time, is able to vote because the annual voters' list is prepared and every voter's name is on the roll. This is a little outside the function of this committee, but it is an interesting point.
In an attempt to finish my remarks quickly, may I simply say that I think this committee has a great and urgent responsibility and that the members of the committee have an opportunity to perform a real service not only to this house but to their country. I might close with a few suggestions that I think are important, not that I think we should be telling the committee what to do but only by way of reviewing some of the things that are being talked about and which have been brought to our attention in the discussions we have had in the last several years. It is just about six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, but I will only take two or three minutes to complete my remarks if I may have that privilege.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understood that a few minutes ago there was unanimous consent to giving the hon. gentleman three or four minutes more, and I hope we are not going to spoil this debate by withdrawing the consent already given. I believe I have an indication that there will probably be only one other speaker who will only be two or three minutes. I think the whole house would feel better if we could get this thing through tonight.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I was attempting to say was not to insult anybody but rather to show that the fault exists in all parts of the house and it is time we put away some of the party differences and party lines that prevent us from functioning more effectively as a parliament. After all, each one of the 265 members of the house has his or her responsibility, and is involved.
I think what we should do is have a vote on interim supply the same day as it is introduced. Likewise, there are repetitious debates on government business that should be avoided. A full scale debate in the resolution stage, and a further wide open debate when a bill is introduced, takes up unnecessary time and is very repetitious.
The period allowed an individual member to speak in debate could likewise be reduced, but very careful attention should be paid to private members' bills. The rights of private members must not only be safeguarded but extended. This applies to a greater use of committees and also to private members' bills. In a modern parliament the backbencher can no longer be relegated to the role of a nonessential appendage.
Another aspect which should be carefully considered is the challenging of the Speaker's
Procedure Committee
decision by an individual member. What we find here is that the right of challenging the Speaker's decision has become a tool for political manoeuvering instead of being the privilege it should be. It would be well for the committee to consider this aspect, particularly in view of the instances which have occurred in the last few weeks, when we have seen misrepresentation to the public, with the obscuring of the real issues originally involved in challenging the Speaker's decision.
During the last two parliaments there has come a greater responsibility upon the opposition in assisting the party with the largest majority, that is the government, to govern. I agree with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) that it is our responsibility in the opposition not just to oppose but to assist the government to govern. Co-operation in the house is not in any way a one-way street.
Some solutions will be very difficult to agree upon, but I trust this committee will at least be able to report on some of the glaring faults in our procedure where unanimity can be achieved. The nation looks expectantly to us to make an honest attempt to correct many of our weaknesses and move forward with the business that we were elected to do. It is our conviction and determination in this party to lend the greatest degree of co-operation we can towards that end.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make several remarks concerning the appointment of a committee on parliamentary procedure but, as it is already after six o'clock and in view of the fact that we shall have the opportunity to express our opinions and to advance arguments in committee, I think that it would be inappropriate to prolong the debate at this time.
We welcome the appointment of this committee on procedure because the procedure in this house has been inadequate for a long time since it does not cover all the events which may occur here. For instance, our group-maybe more than any other-has felt during the last fortnight the effects of that procedure, when events which had not been foreseen, did occur.
Therefore, we hope that, when the committee on procedure meets, it will move the adoption of an order to prevent, from now on, debates as long and as useless as those we have witnessed, when a decision could have been reached much more quickly.
We will support, on this side of the house, the setting up of this committee on procedure in order to give new strength to parliament and do a better job.

Procedure Committee

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to begin a lengthy speech but I hope to make some observations because, of all hon. members in the house, I think I am unique in having occupied positions on both sides of the house and, in addition the chair that Your Honour now occupies.
I do not think this is the time to enter into a litany of those matters where the rules might be amended. I would simply ask, without elaborating at any length, that if rules are to guard against irresponsibility, and we are assured we need more rules, have we therefore become more irresponsible? I do not think so.
I think the rules as they exist could lead to more effective business in the house if they were observed, and the question of observance of the rules is first of all a matter of knowledge of the rules. Here we can all say mea culpa, and some of us can say mea maxima culpa, but then comes the further point, and that is the sense of responsibility in the observance of those rules.
As I have said many times previously, the role of the Chair requires the active co-operation of the house, and if hon. members observed the rules of relevancy I think the problem the Prime Minister indicated about elimination of the resolution stage prior to a bill could be solved. If we were truly relevant we would not have this repetition of debate, because the resolution stage offers the opportunity to put forward alternatives. If we were truly relevant then on second
stage we would stay within the confines of the bill under discussion.
I think the work of the committee will be very interesting, and I hope to be a member of that committee as there are many things on which I have very decided opinions to express.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I have one question with regard to the business for tomorrow. Would the house leader let us know what estimates will be taken up tomorrow night, and also on Friday?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, sir. Tomorrow night we would like to take up the Department of Fisheries and, if it should be concluded before the end of the evening, either the Department of Public Works or the Department of Transport would be available as a stopgap. I will let hon. members know later which one it will be because I have not consulted my colleagues. On Friday evening we will take up the Department of Justice, and the same provision for a second possible department would apply.
I take it, sir, that we could consider there is an order of the house that with the income tax measure, whatever stage we have reached at five o'clock tomorrow would be adjourned until Friday, so that we would quite definitely know we were going into supply at seven o'clock.
It being ten minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
